### Observed differences

- Resource allocation changed for six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22). In the earlier window, each of these activities was handled by a broad mix of resources: the largest single shares were about 5–8 in 100 cases each, and a long tail of occasional resources accounted for roughly 42–48 in 100 cases. In the later window, the frequently used resources are largely different: resources that previously took about 6–8 in 100 cases (including User_16) no longer appear among the main allocators, while a new group (including User_13) takes shares of about 5–9 in 100 cases. [ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A01 shows the sharpest shift: before, its executions were spread over many resources, with a top share of about 7.5 in 100 cases and about 47 in 100 going to the tail; in the later window, every observed A01 execution was assigned to the single resource User_86. [ASSIGN001]
- For most other affected activities, allocation also became somewhat more fragmented: the tail share rose from about 48 to about 56 in 100 cases for A13 and A14, and from about 42 to about 45 in 100 for A22. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN006]
- The allocation profiles for A13 and A14 are identical in both windows, so these two items very likely describe the same underlying behaviour. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- No control-flow or timing indicator passed screening (0 items in each family, against roughly 0.2 and 0.02 expected by chance if nothing had changed), so the flagged differences are confined to resource allocation. [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis of a change in resource allocation: in the earlier window, A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were each executed by a broad mix of resources dominated by one group of codes (including User_16), while in the later window a largely different group (including User_13) took over these activities, and A01 came to be executed exclusively by User_86. Supporting signs: six resource items qualified where about 0.003 would be expected by chance for that family — a count thousands of times the chance expectation — each with an empirical strength of about 0.9995 (the difference exceeds what is seen in about 999.5 of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled traces), and all six point in the same direction with substantial backing (roughly 130–256 traces per activity per window). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, screening]

Limitations: the six items plausibly reflect one underlying reassignment rather than six independent changes (A13 and A14 have identical profiles), and because the resource codes are anonymous, the evidence cannot distinguish a change in allocation rules from a change in which resources were active in each window. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]

Other differences: none qualified — with no control-flow or timing items passing the thresholds, no structural or timing change is supported by this evidence. [screening]
